posts.title: Temporary stability: sequence changes and ad-hoc bracing still create the highest risk
posts.excerpt: CROSS reports continue to highlight the same control failures: late changes to construction sequence that introduce lateral-torsional buckling or loss of restraint, and ad-hoc timber bracing to masonry walls with no design, calculations or competent oversight. Temporary stability belongs on the Temporary Works Register under BS 5975-1:2024 — with a design brief, appropriate check and closed hold points before the temporary condition is created.
posts.linkedinReady:
Temporary stability is not a “construction detail”. It is a temporary works control that must sit on the register under BS 5975-1:2024.

CROSS continues to surface the same pattern. A late change to the construction sequence on a filler-beam bridge deck turned paired beams into individual members and introduced a clear lateral-torsional buckling risk under wet concrete — utilisation well over 100 % without temporary restraint. The Category II checker caught it; the subsequent scramble for bracing, commercial negotiation and restricted working space shows what happens when sequence changes are not routed through the Temporary Works Coordinator and design team early enough.

Separately, CROSS reports persistent use of ad-hoc timber bracing to masonry walls during construction. No design brief, no calculations, no competent oversight. Partially built walls remain vulnerable to modest wind, impact or construction loads. Improvised props give a false sense of security and leave both workers and duty-holders exposed.

The same control gaps appear in recent HSE outcomes: temporary platforms collecting debris with no design or calculated capacity; floors overloaded and not built to the manufacturer’s arrangement; premature loading or removal of support. In every case the item was treated as “just temporary” rather than a structure that must resist foreseeable loads under a managed procedure.

For contractors, site managers and Temporary Works Coordinators this week:
• Capture sequence changes, single-beam lifts, masonry wall restraint and any temporary support to existing structure on the Temporary Works Register immediately.
• Issue a design brief that states the temporary condition, loads and restraints required. Do not accept “we’ll prop it on site”.
• Reject ad-hoc timber bracing or unassessed props. Use designed or justified standard solutions, installed and inspected by competent people, with closed permit-to-load / hold points.
• Ensure the TWC has authority to stop work when the temporary stability assumption changes.
• Confirm that permanent works designers and temporary works designers exchange the information needed for temporary conditions — and that independent checking covers those conditions.

body.h: What CROSS is recording on temporary stability
body.p: CROSS Safety Report 1479 (published January 2026) describes a late change to the intended construction sequence for an approximately 20 m span filler-beam bridge deck. Instead of lifting steel beams in connected pairs (as assumed in the permanent works design), the contractor proposed lifting them individually. This introduced a significant temporary stability concern: lateral-torsional buckling of the unbraced beams under the weight of wet concrete. Analysis showed utilisation factors exceeding 200 % without temporary restraint. The Category II checker identified the risk; the designer confirmed it and required temporary LTB restraints. Subsequent challenges to the necessity of the bracing, compressed design programmes and restricted installation space illustrate the consequences of sequence changes that are not controlled through the Temporary Works Coordinator and design interface. Network Rail has since published engineering advice on consideration of temporary conditions.

CROSS Safety Report 1525 (published May 2026) records ongoing concern about improvised timber bracing systems used to support masonry walls during construction. These arrangements typically lack a temporary works design, calculations or competent oversight. Partially completed masonry walls are vulnerable to overturning under relatively modest loads (wind, impact, construction activity). The reporter notes that such systems are often poorly fixed and create a false sense of security. The Expert Panel observes that temporary stability of masonry during construction is a well-recognised risk and that ad-hoc solutions should be replaced by designed or proven standard systems managed under BS 5975 procedures. Clear identification of the temporary works requirement within trade packages and defined responsibilities for design, installation and inspection are essential.

body.h: The recurring pattern with HSE prosecutions
body.p: Recent HSE outcomes continue to show the same underlying control gaps. Temporary platforms used to collect concrete debris with no design and no calculated safe load (Paxton House, prosecution published June 2026). Floors overloaded with materials and not constructed in accordance with the manufacturer’s design, leading to collapse during bricklaying (Oldham prosecution published August 2026). Premature loading or removal of support, and unprotected openings treated as “just temporary”. In each case the temporary condition was foreseeable and the failure to place the item under a managed temporary works procedure left workers exposed and duty-holders open to enforcement.

body.h: What a competent contractor and TWC should check this week
ul: Walk the Temporary Works Register against any planned sequence changes, single-member lifts, masonry wall construction and temporary support to existing structure; add missing items immediately.
Require a design brief that explicitly states the temporary condition, the loads and restraints that must be present, and the sequence constraints.
Reject ad-hoc timber bracing, unassessed props or improvised stability measures that have no design, check category or competent inspection record.
Ensure the Temporary Works Coordinator has clear authority to stop work when the temporary stability assumption changes and to require re-assessment before work continues.
Confirm information exchange between permanent works designers and temporary works designers for temporary conditions, and that independent checking covers those conditions.
Close permit-to-load / competent inspection hold points before the temporary condition is created or the structure is loaded.

posts.title: Makeshift platforms and unprotected openings: temporary access is still temporary works
posts.excerpt: Two recent HSE prosecutions underline a persistent control gap: operatives on makeshift platforms balanced on stepladders, and falls through unprotected roof lights where no crash deck, edge protection or designed access was in place. Roof and access arrangements belong on the Temporary Works Register under BS 5975-1:2024 — with design brief, appropriate check and closed hold points before people work at height.
posts.linkedinReady:
Two recent HSE prosecutions show why temporary access platforms and openings must be treated as temporary works, not improvisation.

On 18 August 2026 HSE published the outcome against B&O Developers Ltd and its director after public reports of operatives working on a Kings Cross roof with no edge protection and standing on a makeshift platform balanced on a stepladder. Measures identified in the subcontractor risk assessment (including scaffolding) were not in place. The company was fined under the Work at Height Regulations; the director was also sentenced.

Earlier in August, Lowndes Lumb Construction Ltd was fined £60,000 after a worker suffered life-changing injuries falling through an unprotected roof light during domestic refurbishment in Fulham. HSE found no scaffolding, guard rails, internal crash deck or harness systems in use.

These sit alongside the June 2026 Paxton House platform collapse (no design, no calculated safe load for debris platforms) and repeated CROSS material on temporary stability. The common thread is the same: items treated as “just temporary” rather than structures that must resist foreseeable loads under a managed procedure.

For contractors, TWCs and site managers:
• Put roof access, working platforms, crash decks and edge protection on the Temporary Works Register.
• Reject makeshift platforms, unsecured boarding or stepladder improvisations that have no design brief or competent inspection.
• Confirm design or justified standard solution, posted capacity where relevant, and closed permit / inspection hold points before people work at height or over openings.
• Ensure weekly scaffold / platform inspections are completed by a competent person and that changes trigger re-assessment.

body.h: What the recent HSE prosecutions record
body.p: On 18 August 2026 the Health and Safety Executive published the prosecution of B&O Developers Ltd and its sole director following repeated public reports of unsafe roof work during extension and refurbishment of premises on Kings Cross Road, London. Operatives were photographed working on the roof with no edge protection. There was no safe means of access; operatives were seen standing on a makeshift platform balanced on a stepladder. Measures identified as necessary in the roofing subcontractor’s risk assessment, including scaffolding around the roof, were not in place. Despite earlier HSE interventions and meetings, further unsafe work was reported in January 2024. B&O Developers Ltd pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 4(1) of the Work at Height Regulations 2005 and was fined £4,020 plus surcharge. The director pleaded guilty to an offence under Section 37 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 and was fined with costs.

body.h: Unprotected roof light — Fulham, August 2026 outcome
body.p: On 6 August 2026 HSE published the prosecution of Lowndes Lumb Construction Limited after a worker suffered life-changing injuries falling through an unprotected roof light while carrying out roof refurbishment at a domestic property in Fulham on 10 November 2023. The worker was passing materials through an open, unprotected roof light. HSE found that measures to prevent falls — scaffolding, guard rails, an internal crash deck or harness systems — had not been used. The company pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 6(3) of the Work at Height Regulations 2005 and was fined £60,000 plus costs at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on 3 August 2026. Falls from height remain one of the leading causes of workplace death and serious injury.

body.h: Why this is temporary works territory
body.p: Roof access arrangements, working platforms, crash decks over openings and edge protection are temporary works items. They must resist foreseeable loads (people, materials, wind where relevant) and provide a verified load path or containment. BS 5975-1:2024 sets out the management procedure: identify the item, place it on the Temporary Works Register, issue a design brief, obtain an appropriate design and check, permit loading or use only after competent inspection, and maintain control until strike or dismantling. A makeshift platform on a stepladder, unsecured boarding over a roof light, or an inspection form completed by someone not competent for the item does not close the control. The same pattern underpinned the Paxton House temporary platform collapse (prosecution published June 2026): platforms collecting concrete debris with no design and no calculated safe load.

body.h: What a competent contractor and TWC should check this week
ul: Walk the Temporary Works Register against live roof access, working platforms, crash decks over openings and edge protection; add any missing items.
Reject makeshift platforms, stepladder improvisations or unsecured boarding that have no design brief, check category and competent inspection record.
Confirm that design briefs for access platforms and crash decks require assessment of capacity, support conditions and foreseeable loads (people, materials, impact where relevant).
Ensure weekly inspections of scaffolds and platforms are completed by a person competent for the item and that any change triggers re-assessment before further use.
Close permit-to-load / competent inspection hold points before people work at height or over openings.
